chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:

Regarding a man who swore an oath that he would not speak to any of his relatives, he said: It is not binding, so let him speak to the one he swore against. And he said: Every oath in which the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not intended, is not binding regarding divorce or manumission.

He said: And I asked him about a woman who dedicated her wealth as a Hadi (sacrificial animal/gift) for the House of Allah, if she lent her belongings to So-and-so and So-and-so, and some of her family lent them without her command. He said: There is no Hadi upon her. Rather, the Hadi is what is dedicated for Allah as a Hadi for the Kaaba; that is what is fulfilled when dedicated for Allah. And whatever is similar to this is not binding, nor a Hadi, if Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not mentioned in it.
And he was asked about a man who says, 'Upon me is a thousand camels,' and he is in Ihram for a thousand Hajjs. He said: That is from the footsteps of Satan.

And regarding a man who says, and he is in Ihram for a Hajj, he said: It is not binding. Or he says, 'I gift this food,' he said: It is not binding. Indeed, food is not gifted as a Hadi. Or he says, 'The carcass, after it has been slaughtered, I gift it for the House of Allah,' he said: Rather, the camels are gifted while they are alive, and they are not gifted when they have become meat.

key_terms.مُحْرِم: One in the state of Ihram (pilgrimal consecration)

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for an oath or vow to be binding in Shia fiqh, and what constitutes a valid Hadi sacrifice?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principle of 'Yamin al-Ghaws' (excessive or casual oaths) by establishing that oaths lacking sincere intent for Allah's sake are not binding, a key concept in Shia fiqh for distinguishing between binding vows and casual speech. It further refines the jurisprudence of Hadi (sacrificial gift) by specifying that valid offerings must be living animals dedicated specifically to the Kaaba, thereby excluding general gifts or slaughtered meat from this category. These rulings highlight the Shia emphasis on intentionality (niyyah) and precise textual criteria in ritual obligations.
